werk/soundgarden-superunknown.text:
After the tour for Badmotorfinger, Soundgarden began work on a new album in 1993. After two records with Terry Date, the band wanted a different producer and chose Michael Beinhorn. The recording ran from July to September at Bad Animals Studio in Seattle. Each track was recorded separately, with drums and bass first, and the band experimented at length with guitar and drum sounds. Brendan O'Brien mixed the result. There are fifteen tracks on it, because nobody wanted to argue over what had to go.

The album keeps the heaviness of earlier records, but is more varied. There are influences of psychedelia and pop, and Half has an Eastern-tinged atmosphere. Fell on Black Days is in 6/4 time and Limo Wreck in 15/8. Black Hole Sun and Head Down show Beatles influence. Spoonman and Black Hole Sun won a Grammy. The record was the band's breakthrough and is regarded as a grunge classic.
werk/soundgarden-superunknown.listen: Listen to the slow, heavy rhythm of Fell on Black Days, which runs in 6/4. Try to notice how the time signature carries the song's gloom.

werk/stan-getz-focus.text:
In 1960 Stan Getz was living in Denmark and struggling with addiction. New jazz by Miles Davis, John Coltrane and Ornette Coleman stimulated him, and in January 1961 he returned to the United States. His label wanted commercial music, but he wanted a more personal album. He therefore asked the arranger Eddie Sauter for a series of seven pieces, entirely original music and no standards. The recording sessions in July 1961 began without him, because his mother had died the day before. He later played his parts in, wearing headphones, over the strings that had already been recorded.

The saxophonist improvised freely on Sauter's themes instead of on chord changes. Roy Haynes is the only other soloist, in I'm Late, I'm Late, which was edited together from two takes. Getz later called Focus his favourite record. The Penguin Guide to Jazz included the album in its core selection, and a biographer spoke of the best-realised third stream record ever.
werk/stan-getz-focus.listen: Listen to I'm Late, I'm Late for the interplay of the tenor saxophone with the strings, and for the solo by drummer Roy Haynes.

werk/stan-getz-getz-gilberto.text:
By 1962 Stan Getz had already made two bossa nova records, including Jazz Samba, and producer Creed Taylor wanted him to collaborate with the creators of the genre. So in March 1963, at A & R Recording Studios in New York, in two days, a record was made with the Brazilian singer and guitarist João Gilberto and the pianist and composer Antônio Carlos Jobim. Phil Ramone was the engineer and Verve released the album in March 1964. The rhythm section consisted of Jobim, bassist Sebastião Neto and drummer Milton Banana.

On two songs, Garota de Ipanema and Corcovado, Astrud Gilberto sings. The Girl from Ipanema won a Grammy for Record of the Year and launched her career. Critics praised the bossa nova groove and the minimalism of the record. The album also won the Grammy for Album of the Year, as the first non-American record ever, and is seen as the record that made bossa nova popular worldwide.
werk/stan-getz-getz-gilberto.listen: Listen to The Girl from Ipanema and notice how Getz's saxophone and Astrud Gilberto's voice alternate over a gentle bossa nova rhythm.

werk/stan-getz-hamp-and-getz.text:
Hamp and Getz is an album by vibraphonist Lionel Hampton and tenor saxophonist Stan Getz, recorded in 1955 and released on the Norgran label. Producer Norman Granz brought together two parties who at first sight seemed ill-matched: the cool Getz and the extrovert Hampton. Pianist Lou Levy, bassist Leroy Vinnegar and drummer Shelly Manne make up the rhythm section.

The repertoire runs from Cherokee and a ballad medley to Count Basie's Jumpin' at the Woodside and Hampton's Gladys. Billboard wrote at the end of December 1955 that Hampton was the stronger of the two and that Getz, under his influence, played more roughly and with less inhibition than usual. AllMusic gave it four and a half stars and called it classic music by two outstanding players.
werk/stan-getz-hamp-and-getz.listen: Listen to Cherokee for the interplay of vibraphone and tenor saxophone, and notice how Getz sounds rougher than you are used to from him.

werk/stan-getz-the-brothers.text:
The Brothers is a compilation album by the saxophonists Stan Getz and Zoot Sims, which Prestige released in 1956. The four recordings of 8 April 1949 had already appeared on separate records, under the name Stan Getz Tenor Sax Stars. In 1956 Prestige put them together into an album for the first time and added four pieces by Zoot Sims and Al Cohn. Later the album was reissued many times, and on CD three alternate takes from the vaults were added.

Three tenor saxophonists play on the 1949 recordings: Getz, Allen Eager and Brew Moore. Sims and Cohn play on the later pieces. The music recalls the light Four Brothers sound that the tenor saxophonists had shown in Woody Herman's band in 1947. A reviewer at AllMusic called it a fine record that shows the cool, early West Coast bop of these soloists and of Miles Davis.
werk/stan-getz-the-brothers.listen: Listen to Five Brothers and notice the different tenor saxophonists and how light their sound is.

werk/stan-getz-west-coast-jazz.text:
West Coast Jazz is an album from 1955 by Stan Getz with a quartet that also includes trumpeter Conte Candoli. Getz recorded the record in California, where he was filming scenes for The Benny Goodman Story and played for a week at Zardi's Jazzland. He also chose the musicians who accompanied him there for the album. The producer was Norman Granz and David Stone Martin drew the cover.

The title is a joke, because Getz did not belong to the West Coast style. Al Campbell of AllMusic in fact heard strong group playing with energetic bop solos, especially in S-H-I-N-E and Dizzy Gillespie's A Night in Tunisia. Billboard called the record a smash in October 1955, one that swings powerfully. In 1996 the album was reissued on Verve with extra tracks.
werk/stan-getz-west-coast-jazz.listen: Listen to Night in Tunisia for the fast interplay between the tenor saxophone and the rest of the group.

werk/stan-kenton-city-of-glass.text:
City of Glass was released as a ten-inch LP by Stan Kenton and consists entirely of music by Bob Graettinger. Kenton had re-formed his orchestra in September 1947 to play progressive jazz for the concert hall. In December 1951 a new Innovations Orchestra was given two studio days, entirely devoted to Graettinger. The main work is the four-part suite City of Glass, a rewritten version of a composition from 1948 that had been performed only twice, in Chicago.

Incident in Jazz is regarded as Graettinger's most coherent work. Opinions on his music were divided. Trumpeter Buddy Childers called it nonsense, and Kenton himself said it was either the best music the orchestra had ever played, or the biggest mess. Graettinger died in 1957, aged 33.
werk/stan-kenton-city-of-glass.listen: Listen to Incident In Jazz for the irregular structure, without fixed symmetry, and for how the work ends quietly.

werk/stan-kenton-contemporary-concepts.text:
Contemporary Concepts is an album of jazz standards that Stan Kenton recorded in 1955 and released on Capitol. Kenton leads the orchestra and plays piano. Bill Holman wrote the arrangements for the first six tracks, including What's New, Stella by Starlight and Cherokee, and Gerry Mulligan arranged his own Limelight.

The orchestra includes soloists such as altoists Charlie Mariano and Lennie Niehaus, tenor saxophonist Bill Perkins, trombonist Carl Fontana and trumpeters Sam Noto and Stu Williamson. Drummer Mel Lewis drives the rhythm section along. The reviewer Scott Yanow felt that the music swings well and that nothing very innovative happens, but that this accessible record is of interest to lovers of bop.
werk/stan-kenton-contemporary-concepts.listen: Listen to Stella By Starlight and notice how Mel Lewis's drums push the rhythm section along.

werk/stan-kenton-portraits-on-standards.text:
In 1953 Stan Kenton and his orchestra recorded a series of jazz standards for Capitol, which first appeared on a 10-inch LP. The arrangements were written by Bill Russo. Kenton himself led the group and played piano. The orchestra included, among others, Conte Candoli, Frank Rosolino, Lee Konitz and Zoot Sims.

The album features songs such as I've Got You Under My Skin, April in Paris, How High the Moon, Crazy Rhythm and Duke Ellington's I Got It Bad. According to the reviewer Scott Yanow, most of this orchestra's recordings from the 1950s were complicated and sometimes bombastic, but the versions of standards were often sentimental and very melodic. The music alternates, in his view, between ballads and boppish outbursts from an orchestra that could swing hard.
werk/stan-kenton-portraits-on-standards.listen: Listen to April in Paris and notice how melodic Bill Russo's arrangement sounds.

werk/stanley-clarke-children-of-forever.text:
Stanley Clarke recorded his debut album in December 1972. Polydor Records released it in 1973. Chick Corea produced it and also played on it, on electric piano, piano and clavinet. Also heard were, among others, guitarist Pat Martino, drummer Lenny White, flautist Arthur Webb and the singers Dee Dee Bridgewater and Andy Bey.

The album has only five tracks, and they are long: Children of Forever lasts over ten minutes and Sea Journey, which Corea wrote with Neville Potter, over sixteen. The lyrics are by Potter. Billboard wrote that avant garde and funk come together here, with Andy Bey as a strong voice and Corea on electric piano. Thom Jurek of AllMusic thinks the record has aged excellently and is full of heart and inspiration.
werk/stanley-clarke-children-of-forever.listen: Listen to Sea Journey, the longest track on the record, and notice how much time it takes to develop.

werk/stanley-clarke-journey-to-love.text:
Journey to Love is the third solo album by the jazz fusion bassist Stanley Clarke. He plays bass guitar, double bass and piccolo bass himself, also plays organ, bells and gong, and sings. He brought many well-known guests into the studio. Jeff Beck plays electric guitar on Hello Jeff and a guitar solo on the title track. Chick Corea plays piano and John McLaughlin acoustic guitar on Song to John.

George Duke plays keyboards and sings, David Sancious plays guitar and Steve Gadd drums. Lenny White drums on Hello Jeff. There is also a brass section including trumpeters Jon Faddis and Lew Soloff. The album closes with the Concerto for Jazz/Rock Orchestra.
werk/stanley-clarke-journey-to-love.listen: Listen to Hello Jeff and notice the interplay of the bass with Jeff Beck's electric guitar.

werk/stargate-irreplaceable.text: On 17 October 2006 Irreplaceable by Beyoncé was released. It was made by the Norwegian production duo Stargate, with singer Ne-Yo as lyricist. Ne-Yo had first intended it as a country song. Stargate and Beyoncé turned it into an R&B song, with the acoustic guitar still up front. It spent ten weeks at number one in America. As in Sweden, American hits now also came from Norway.
werk/stargate-irreplaceable.listen: Hear the acoustic guitar under the beat: a trace of the country song it first was.

werk/steel-pulse-caught-you.text:
Caught You is the third album by the reggae band Steel Pulse and was released in 1980. In the United States it came out under the title Reggae Fever. It was the band's last album for Island Records. Singer and guitarist David Hinds wrote almost all the songs.

The ten songs still carry heavy messages, for example in Harassment and Nyahbinghi Voyage, but a reviewer at AllMusic noted that the band's jazz leanings were now in the foreground. Trouser Press called the record Steel Pulse at its most pop-oriented, while also finding the lyrics too often preachy and clichéd.
werk/steel-pulse-caught-you.listen: Listen to Harassment and notice how a serious message is delivered here by a band that also shows jazzy colours.

werk/steel-pulse-handsworth-revolution.text:
Handsworth Revolution is the debut album by Steel Pulse, named after the district of Handsworth in Birmingham, where the band comes from and to which the record is dedicated. It was released in 1978 on Island Records, after the first single Ku Klux Klan, a call to resist racism. Producer Karl Pitterson had previously worked with Bob Marley, Bunny Wailer and Peter Tosh.

The album received glowing reviews and ten days after its release stood at number 9 on the British chart. In the summer of 1978 the group played as the support act for Bob Marley and the Wailers in Europe and learned stage discipline there. At a Rock Against Racism performance in Victoria Park, more than 80,000 people watched. The singles Prodigal Son and Prediction also came from the album. Mykaell Riley left the band afterwards.
werk/steel-pulse-handsworth-revolution.listen: Listen to Ku Klux Klan and notice the message of resistance in the lyrics and how it is delivered over a reggae rhythm.

werk/steel-pulse-tribute-to-the-martyrs.text:
Tribute to the Martyrs is the second studio album by the English reggae band Steel Pulse and was released in July 1979. It reached number 42 on the British album chart and number 36 in Sweden. Almost all the songs were written by singer David Hinds. Only Babylon Makes the Rules comes from keyboardist Selwyn Brown.

Two songs have a clear social theme. Biko's Kindred Lament is a tribute to Steve Biko, the South African anti-apartheid activist. Jah Pickney R.A.R. is about Rock Against Racism. Brass also plays on the album: a saxophone, a flugelhorn, a cornet and a trombone. The record contains eight songs, of which Blasphemy (Selah) at seven minutes is the longest, and the title song follows with almost seven.
werk/steel-pulse-tribute-to-the-martyrs.listen: Listen to Biko's Kindred Lament and notice the atmosphere of a tribute to Steve Biko.

werk/steely-dan-aja.text:
For this sixth album, Steely Dan, under bandleaders Walter Becker and Donald Fagen, had themselves surrounded again and again by different session musicians: almost forty in total. The compositions grew longer and more refined. The producer was, as on all the earlier records, Gary Katz. The title piece consists of sections that had been written separately from one another, with solos by saxophonist Wayne Shorter and drummer Steve Gadd. On Home at Last, Bernard Purdie played his own Purdie Shuffle. Peg was the last track and the only one recorded in New York.

Aja was released on 23 September 1977 on ABC Records and became the group's most commercially successful album, with the hits Peg, Deacon Blues and Josie. It received a Grammy for engineering, and many critics and audiophiles praise the quality of the production. In 2010 the Library of Congress included it in the National Recording Registry.
werk/steely-dan-aja.listen: Listen to Home at Last and notice Bernard Purdie's half-time shuffle rhythm: funky and relaxed, but different from the ordinary shuffles of that period.

werk/steely-dan-can-t-buy-a-thrill.text:
As Steely Dan's debut, this album was released in October 1972 on ABC Records. Walter Becker and Donald Fagen wrote all the songs and recorded them in August at the Village Recorder in Los Angeles, with producer Gary Katz. Some of the songs the duo had written before their move to California, such as Midnite Cruiser and Brooklyn. Singer David Palmer was recruited during the sessions, because Fagen did not want to sing live, and sang lead on two tracks.

The album is stylistically varied, with soft rock, pop, Latin rhythms and a cautious jazz touch. Do It Again has a tight Latin-jazz beat and Reelin' In the Years features jazzy guitar solos and harmonies. The lyrics are philosophical and somewhat cryptic. The record received good reviews, produced two successful singles and later appeared in several lists of the best albums.
werk/steely-dan-can-t-buy-a-thrill.listen: Listen to Do It Again and notice the Latin beat and how the vocals come calmly over it.

werk/steely-dan-countdown-to-ecstasy.text:
Steely Dan's second album was recorded between tours at Village Recorder in West Los Angeles. Singer David Palmer had left, so Donald Fagen sings all the songs. Because there was little time, songs were often made at the last minute: Fagen wrote Bodhisattva the evening before the recording. Only eight songs were recorded. In Bodhisattva he played all four parts of a saxophone-like section one by one on an ARP synthesizer. Afterwards he threw the instrument down the stairs and set it on fire.

The style is rock with a strong jazz influence. Most songs last longer than five minutes and are subtle in texture. Razor Boy rests on a reggae beat. My Old School tells of a drug raid at Bard College in 1969, in which the writers were arrested. The album was a critical success, but produced no hit in America. It reached number 35 and went gold in 1978.
werk/steely-dan-countdown-to-ecstasy.listen: Listen to the instrumental section in Bodhisattva, where four synthesizer parts sound like a saxophone section.

werk/steely-dan-katy-lied.text:
Katy Lied came out in March 1975 on ABC Records. It was the first album after Walter Becker and Donald Fagen decided to stop touring and concentrate on the studio. Guitarists Jeff Baxter and Denny Dias and drummer Jim Hodder left the group; Becker called it liberating that he could stop such difficult collaborations. From then on they worked with studio musicians. Dias stayed on as a session musician, Michael Omartian played most of the keyboards and the twenty-year-old Jeff Porcaro the drums on almost all the tracks. He struggled with Your Gold Teeth II, which changes time signature, until Fagen gave him an album by Charles Mingus. Michael McDonald made his debut here with backing vocals.

Phil Woods played his saxophone solo in Doctor Wu in one take. Black Friday reached number 37 on the American chart, but Bad Sneakers is now the best-known song. The album reached thirteenth place and went gold.
werk/steely-dan-katy-lied.listen: Listen to Doctor Wu and notice Phil Woods's saxophone solo, which was recorded in one go.

werk/steely-dan-pretzel-logic.text:
Pretzel Logic was recorded at the Village Recorder in Los Angeles under producer Gary Katz and was the group's last record as a touring band. Walter Becker and Donald Fagen wrote the songs and brought in well-known studio musicians to perform them, so that the other band members had less to do. Because new songs were hard to come by, they used three older songs and, for the only time, covered a piece by Duke Ellington.

The songs are shorter than on the previous record and fit the three-minute format, with funk in Night by Night and a shuffle in the title track. Rikki Don't Lose That Number opens with a syncopated piano line and borrows the bass part from Horace Silver's Song for My Father. Parker's Band is a tribute to Charlie Parker. The album was a success with critics and public, and Rikki became the group's biggest hit. After that, Becker and Fagen stopped touring.
werk/steely-dan-pretzel-logic.listen: Listen to the syncopated piano line with which Rikki Don't Lose That Number opens, and notice how it turns into a pop melody.

werk/steely-dan-the-royal-scam.text:
The Royal Scam came out in May 1976 on ABC Records and, like all the earlier albums, was produced by Gary Katz. Whereas the previous and following records were mainly jazz rock, this is chiefly a funk album. Recording began in Los Angeles with engineer Elliot Scheiner, but after two weeks with all kinds of session musicians, Walter Becker and Donald Fagen were still not satisfied. They moved to New York, where half the backing tracks were made, including that of Kid Charlemagne in one take. The recording process with two linked 16-track recorders proved hard to edit, after which they returned to Los Angeles and Roger Nichols became the engineer again.

Haitian Divorce is based on Scheiner's trip to Haiti to get a divorce. The single reached number 17 in England and is the highest position outside America. The album reached number 15 in the United States, went platinum and reached number 11 in England.
werk/steely-dan-the-royal-scam.listen: Listen to Kid Charlemagne and notice the rhythm section, which was made in a single take. Hear how the funk keeps running through the whole song.

werk/steely-dan-two-against-nature.text:
Twenty years after their previous studio album, Steely Dan came back in 2000 with Two Against Nature, the band's eighth album. It was recorded from 1997 to 1999 and released on 29 February 2000 on Giant Records. Donald Fagen sang and played keyboards, Walter Becker bass and guitar.

Critics heard a bouncier and sharper sound than on Aja from 1977, a jazz pop that Robert Christgau called post-funk. The lyrics are about older men seeking validation and excitement in their love lives, with a sharp humour. The album won four Grammys, including Album of the Year, and Cousin Dupree earned the award for best pop performance by a duo or group. It reached number six on the American chart and went platinum. The tour of North America, Europe and Japan was just as successful.
werk/steely-dan-two-against-nature.listen: Listen to Cousin Dupree, the song that won a Grammy, and notice how it sounds: what are the instruments doing alongside the vocals?

werk/steve-cropper-jammed-together.text:
In May 1969 Stax released twenty-seven albums at once, to celebrate its tenth anniversary and a new distribution deal. Jammed Together was one of them. It brings together the label's three best-known guitarists: bluesman Albert King, gospel singer Pops Staples and Steve Cropper of Booker T. and the M.G.'s. It looks like a jam session, but according to Cropper they were never in the studio together. Stax boss Al Bell had them record their parts separately, because they were all busy.

The music is largely instrumental and mixes blues, soul and gospel with a hefty rock beat. Each guitarist sings one song. King takes the lead with his bent notes, Cropper plays more quietly, and Staples provides gospel-style tremolo. There are covers such as What'd I Say and Baby, What You Want Me to Do. Critics later called it filler for the guitar market, but some especially praised Opus de Soul.
werk/steve-cropper-jammed-together.listen: Listen to What'd I Say and try to tell the three guitars apart. Notice how they alternate and complement each other.

werk/stevie-nicks-bella-donna.text:
Bella Donna is Stevie Nicks's first solo album. She began it in 1979, between the recording of Fleetwood Mac's Tusk, and worked on it after the tour with a full band under producer Jimmy Iovine. The record was recorded bit by bit, because session musicians such as Waddy Wachtel and Russ Kunkel had little time. Without Lindsey Buckingham, she let the musicians fill in for themselves what they heard on her demos. Friends such as Tom Petty and Don Henley sang along.

Stop Draggin' My Heart Around with Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers became a hit, as did Leather and Lace with Henley, Edge of Seventeen and the country-flavoured After the Glitter Fades. The album reached number one on the American chart. Critics were divided. Rolling Stone praised the arrangements, while Record Mirror found the record too well-behaved. AllMusic later wrote that Iovine kept the sound organic.
werk/stevie-nicks-bella-donna.listen: Listen to Edge of Seventeen and notice the guitar and the rhythm that drive the song forward.

werk/stevie-nicks-the-wild-heart.text:
The Wild Heart is Stevie Nicks's second solo album, released on 10 June 1983. Recording began at the end of 1982, shortly after Fleetwood Mac's Mirage Tour. Her best friend Robin Anderson had died, and that gave her a new awareness of what her life and work were worth. In a few months the record was finished.

An unusually large number of guests played on it. Tom Petty wrote I Will Run to You, on which his Heartbreakers play. Steve Lukather of Toto played guitar on Stand Back, the album's biggest hit, with an uncredited synthesizer part by Prince. Beauty and the Beast closes with strings conducted by Paul Buckmaster. Billboard found the record harder-rocking than its predecessor Bella Donna. AllMusic wrote that anyone who loved Bella Donna would love this record too.
werk/stevie-nicks-the-wild-heart.listen: Listen to Stand Back and notice the synthesizer part, on which Prince played uncredited.

werk/stevie-wonder-fulfillingness-first-.text:
Fulfillingness' First Finale was released on 22 July 1974 on Tamla, a subsidiary label of Motown. It was Stevie Wonder's seventeenth studio album and the fourth from his so-called classic period. His previous record Innervisions had a grand scale and a social theme. This album sounds more personal, reflective and sombre.

Many arrangements are sparse, especially in They Won't Go When I Go and the restrained Creepin'. Yet the social criticism did not disappear: You Haven't Done Nothin' went to number 1 on the American chart and contains a sharp indictment of the Nixon administration, with clavinet, a drum machine and a guest appearance by the Jackson 5. The album spent two weeks at the top of the American album chart and won three Grammys, including Album of the Year, for the second time in a row.
werk/stevie-wonder-fulfillingness-first-.listen: Listen to Creepin' and notice how few instruments are needed and how restrained the song sounds as a result.

werk/stevie-wonder-hotter-than-july.text:
After the commercial and critical disappointment of Journey Through The Secret Life of Plants from 1979, Stevie Wonder was in a difficult period. He wrote, arranged and produced Hotter Than July himself, mostly at Wonderland Studios in Los Angeles, which he had just bought. The album was released on 29 September 1980 on Tamla. Master Blaster (Jammin') was inspired by the reggae of Bob Marley, whom he had met in 1979. Other successes were I Ain't Gonna Stand for It, the ballad Lately and the cheerful Happy Birthday. On All I Do, among others, Michael Jackson sang along.

He wrote Happy Birthday in honour of Martin Luther King and used it to campaign for a national holiday on his birthday. The sleeve, too, was devoted to that. The album reached number three in America and went platinum. In England it was his most successful record, with four singles in the top ten.
werk/stevie-wonder-hotter-than-july.listen: Listen to Happy Birthday and notice how cheerful it sounds, while the song had a serious purpose: campaigning for a holiday in honour of Martin Luther King.

werk/stevie-wonder-innervisions.text:
After Music of My Mind and Talking Book, Stevie Wonder was increasingly seen in the music world as a master of the album format. For this album he again worked with the synthesizers of Malcolm Cecil and Robert Margouleff, who also urged him to sing not only about love but also about political and spiritual themes. Lyrics, music and production are almost entirely his own, and on many tracks he plays nearly all the instruments.

The nine songs deal with drugs in Too High, with inequality and racism in Living for the City and with love in All in Love Is Fair and Golden Lady. Living for the City is regarded as the centrepiece and uses street sounds such as traffic, voices and sirens between the studio music. The album came out in August 1973. Three days later Wonder was seriously injured in a car accident. It won a Grammy for album of the year and influenced later soul.
werk/stevie-wonder-innervisions.listen: Listen to the street sounds between the music in Living for the City, and notice how angry Wonder sounds in the last verse.

werk/stevie-wonder-music-of-my-mind.text:
Music of My Mind was released on 3 March 1972 on Tamla. It was Stevie Wonder's first album under a new contract with Motown, which gave him complete artistic freedom. After a meeting in May 1971 with the electronic musicians Malcolm Cecil and Robert Margouleff, he began working with ARP and Moog synthesizers. They were co-producers and helped build the sound, with their own synthesizer TONTO. Wonder produced it himself and played nearly all the instruments himself, apart from the trombone in Love Having You Around and the guitar in Superwoman.

Critics saw the album as a step towards artistic maturity. Keep On Running was praised for its Moog work. Some reviewers found the studio and vocal effects a little too much of a good thing. The album reached sixth place on the R&B chart and twenty-first on the pop chart. Today it is regarded as the first album of Wonder's classic period.
werk/stevie-wonder-music-of-my-mind.listen: Listen to Keep On Running and notice the Moog bass and synthesizer sounds. Try to hear how a single musician makes a whole band sound with them.

werk/stevie-wonder-stevie-at-the-beach.text:
Stevie at the Beach was released on 23 June 1964 on Motown's Tamla label. It is Stevie Wonder's fourth studio album. The album is a kind of concept album built around beach music and surf songs. The label wanted to have him sing surf numbers as well. Motown had earlier tried to turn him into a teenage version of Ray Charles, and for one album a lounge singer.

Wonder sings and plays harmonica, drums and keyboards, and various session musicians from Los Angeles play along. The record includes Castles in the Sand, Ebb Tide, Beach Stomp and Beyond the Sea. Only Hey Harmonica Man was a modest hit. The rest did not catch on with the public. Only in 1965 did Wonder have a hit again, when he was allowed to show more of his musical talent.
werk/stevie-wonder-stevie-at-the-beach.listen: Listen to the harmonica in Hey Harmonica Man, an instrument that Wonder plays himself on this album.

werk/stevie-wonder-talking-book.text:
In 1972 Stevie Wonder made two albums in quick succession: Music of My Mind and Talking Book. Together they open his classic period. He had more artistic freedom from Motown and leaned less on Berry Gordy. He played most of it himself, with help from guests such as Jeff Beck and David Sanborn. Robert Margouleff and Malcolm Cecil helped with a production style in which layers of keyboards and synthesizers took the place of strings.

The sound is defined by keyboards. In Superstition the clavinet is regarded as one of the defining examples of the instrument, and in Big Brother it sounds like an acoustic guitar. The lyrics are about love, but also about politics and society. You Are the Sunshine of My Life and Superstition went to number one in America, and the album brought Wonder his first Grammy. It often appears on lists of the best albums of all time.
werk/stevie-wonder-talking-book.listen: Listen to Superstition and notice the rhythm of the clavinet, which sharply and funkily carries the whole song.

werk/stevie-wonder-the-jazz-soul-of-litt.text:
The Jazz Soul of Little Stevie is the debut album of Little Stevie Wonder and was released in September 1962 on Tamla Records. He was twelve then and mainly showed what he could do as a composer and instrumentalist. He does not sing on this album. He plays percussion, keyboards and harmonica. Clarence Paul and Henry Cosby wrote and produced most of it, and he co-wrote two songs.

The album contains the original studio version of Fingertips. The live version of it would later become his first hit. Bruce Eder of AllMusic praised the record as a stunning document and called the young musician exceptional as a drummer, bongo player, harmonica player, keyboardist and composer. Much of the instrumental music was very sophisticated for its time, and the reference to jazz in the title was, in his view, no exaggeration: a large part is real jazz.
werk/stevie-wonder-the-jazz-soul-of-litt.listen: Listen to Fingertips (Original Studio Session) and notice the harmonica playing and the percussion of this twelve-year-old.

werk/stevie-wonder-tribute-to-uncle-ray.text:
Tribute to Uncle Ray is the second studio album by Little Stevie Wonder and was released by Motown in October 1962, shortly after The Jazz Soul of Little Stevie. Yet it was the first to be recorded, when he was eleven. Berry Gordy and Motown wanted to link the young singer with Ray Charles, who, like him, was blind and African American.

The songs are almost all by Ray Charles, such as Hallelujah I Love Her So, Come Back Baby and Drown in My Own Tears. In addition there are songs by others, such as (I'm Afraid) The Masquerade Is Over, and Sunset, which he wrote with Clarence Paul under the name Stevie Judkins. Like his debut, the album produced no hits. Motown was still searching for a sound that suited the twelve-year-old singer.
werk/stevie-wonder-tribute-to-uncle-ray.listen: Listen to Hallelujah I Love Her So and notice how a young voice sings a Ray Charles song.

werk/sting-nothing-like-the-sun.text:
Nothing Like the Sun is Sting's second solo album and came out on 16 October 1987 on A&M. He recorded it between March and August 1987 at AIR Studios on Montserrat, with Bryan Loren and Neil Dorfsman as producers. Two events colour the record: the death of his mother in June 1987 and his participation in Amnesty International's Conspiracy of Hope Tour, where he met victims of oppression. From that came They Dance Alone, about Chilean women who dance the cueca alone with photographs of the disappeared on their clothes.

The title comes from Shakespeare's Sonnet 130, which appears in Sister Moon. Englishman in New York is a tribute to Quentin Crisp and sounds jazzy. The record received favourable reviews, won the Brit Award for best British album in 1988 and in 1989 stood at number 90 on Rolling Stone's list of the best albums of the 1980s.
werk/sting-nothing-like-the-sun.listen: Listen to Englishman in New York and notice how jazz influences give the pop song an elegant, relaxed colour.

werk/sting-ten-summoner-s-tales.text:
Ten Summoner's Tales is Sting's fourth solo album and came out in 1993. After the heavy, introspective predecessor The Soul Cages, he wanted to write lighter music, songs that would amuse his band and family. They are about love and morality. He recorded the record in his own studio at Lake House in Wiltshire, with Hugh Padgham as co-producer. The title is a pun on his surname Sumner and the summoner from Chaucer's The Canterbury Tales.

The music plays with time signatures: Love Is Stronger Than Justice (The Munificent Seven) is written in 7/4, a nod to the films Seven Samurai and The Magnificent Seven, and Seven Days in 5/4. If I Ever Lose My Faith in You and Fields of Gold were hits in the United States. The album was nominated for six Grammys and made the shortlist for the Mercury Prize.
werk/sting-ten-summoner-s-tales.listen: Listen to Seven Days and try to hear that this song is in 5/4, a time signature in which the count doesn't quite come out neatly on four.

werk/sting-the-dream-of-the-blue-turtles.text:
The Dream of the Blue Turtles is Sting's first solo album, released on 17 June 1985. The title comes from a dream of the singer himself. At first he worked with the producers of Torch Song on synthesizer-driven electrofunk, but in the end he did not choose that. In January 1985 he held auditions for jazz musicians in New York and brought in, among others, Omar Hakim, Branford Marsalis, Kenny Kirkland and Darryl Jones. The band recorded for seven weeks at Blue Wave Studio in Barbados.

The record mixes pop and jazz. Russians is about the fear of nuclear weapons in the Cold War, We Work the Black Seam about the miners' strike of 1984 and 1985, and Moon Over Bourbon Street is inspired by a novel by Anne Rice. Critics were full of praise. The album received Grammy nominations, including for Album of the Year.
werk/sting-the-dream-of-the-blue-turtles.listen: Listen to Moon Over Bourbon Street and notice the double bass and the dark atmosphere of the song.

werk/sting-the-soul-cages.text:
The Soul Cages is Sting's third studio album and was released on 21 January 1991. It is a concept album about the death of his father Ernest Sumner. After that death in 1987, Sting developed a writer's block that lasted for years. He broke it by working through his father's death in music. Many songs are about sailing and the sea, and refer to Newcastle, where he grew up. He started from the image of an enormous ship above the house, next to the shipyard.

Because he had no finished songs, he worked them out in the studio with guitarist Dominic Miller, keyboardist Kenny Kirkland and drummer Manu Katché. The basic tracks took six weeks in Paris. The title song won the first Grammy for Best Rock Song in 1992.
werk/sting-the-soul-cages.listen: Listen to The Wild Wild Sea and notice how the sea theme, which runs through the whole album, returns in this song.

werk/suicidal-tendencies-controlled-by-h.text:
This fourth album by Suicidal Tendencies came out on 17 October 1989 on Epic and has an unusual structure. It is divided into two invented EPs: the first four songs are called Controlled by Hatred and the remaining five Feel Like Shit… Deja‐Vu. It contains new versions of songs by No Mercy, the former band of guitarist Mike Clark, a cover of Los Cycos and two versions of How Will I Laugh Tomorrow.

Because the record contains re-recordings, it was called a compilation or double EP. Yet it counts as a studio album. The band had no permanent bassist: the bass parts were played by the guitarists Rocky George and Mike Clark. The Heavy Emotion Version of How Will I Laugh Tomorrow is almost acoustic, with a solo from George all the same. It was the first of two albums by the band to go gold.
werk/suicidal-tendencies-controlled-by-h.listen: Listen to How Will I Laugh Tomorrow (Heavy Emotion Version) and notice how soft and almost acoustic it sounds, with a guitar solo all the same.

werk/suicidal-tendencies-how-will-i-laug.text:
This third album by Suicidal Tendencies was released on 13 September 1988 on Epic Records, the first for that label. New was rhythm guitarist Mike Clark, who had previously played with singer Mike Muir in No Mercy and wrote much of the music. Bob Heathcote played bass, on this album only. It was recorded at Cherokee Studios in Hollywood under Mark Dodson.

The band left most of the punk influences behind and chose a sound that was more thrash, with longer and more complex songs and better production. Rocky George was given more room for solos. Trip at the Brain and the title track became singles that struck a chord with their target audience. Reviews were mostly positive. The album reached position 111 on the American chart, and Revolver later placed it among the essential thrash records.
werk/suicidal-tendencies-how-will-i-laug.listen: Listen to How Will I Laugh Tomorrow and notice what the guitars do alongside Mike Muir's vocals.

werk/suicidal-tendencies-join-the-army.text:
Join the Army, released in April 1987, is the second album by Suicidal Tendencies. It is one of the best-known records combining punk and thrash metal, a style known as crossover thrash, for which the band is seen as a co-inventor. The producers were Lester Claypool and the band themselves, at the Record Plant in Los Angeles. Two new members played on it: guitarist Rocky George, who pushed the sound towards thrash, and drummer R.J. Herrera, who used a double bass drum. It was also the last record with bassist Louiche Mayorga.

Singer Mike Muir used very different vocal techniques than on the debut and sometimes sounded like Lemmy of Motörhead. The single Possessed to Skate was given a music video with old skateboard tricks, which is regarded as a snapshot of skating in its day. AllMusic called the record a transitional album from hardcore punk to thrash. It reached position 100 on the Billboard 200 and drew the attention of major labels. Epic signed the band in 1988.
werk/suicidal-tendencies-join-the-army.listen: Listen to Possessed to Skate and notice the fast guitar work and the double bass drum, which lift the punk sound towards metal.

werk/sun-ra-cosmos.text:
Cosmos is an album by Sun Ra and his Arkestra, recorded in 1976 in France. It was released on the French label Cobra in Europe and on Inner City Records in the United States. Sun Ra wrote all the pieces himself and here plays Rocksichord, an electric keyboard instrument. He leads a band that includes John Gilmore on tenor saxophone, Marshall Allen and Danny Davis on alto saxophone and flute, and also trumpet, horn, trombone, bassoon, bass clarinet and electric bass.

The titles point to outer space: Interstellar Low Ways, Moonship Journey, Journey Among the Stars and Jazz from an Unknown Planet. Ron Wynn of AllMusic wrote that Sun Ra plays beautiful moments on the Rocksichord. The Arkestra plays stomping, atmospheric numbers or hard bop, and in them various saxophonists briefly come to the fore in dialogues that sound fast, screaming and sometimes spacey.
werk/sun-ra-cosmos.listen: Listen to Jazz from an Unknown Planet to hear how the horns alternate and respond to each other over the band's rhythm.

werk/sun-ra-space-is-the-place.text:
Space Is the Place by Sun Ra was released in 1973 on the Blue Thumb label. In 1998 Impulse! Records reissued the album. Stephen Cook of AllMusic called it an excellent introduction to Sun Ra's extensive, free jazz catalogue, and a recommendation for lovers of Sun Ra.

The title song is described by the BBC as his ultimate anthem. In that song, science fiction and ancient myth come together with everything jazz has to offer. That combination also appealed to rock bands, such as the MC5, Sonic Youth and Primal Scream, who were at the forefront of rock.
werk/sun-ra-space-is-the-place.listen: Listen to Space Is the Place and notice how the song connects a science fiction theme with jazz.

werk/sun-ra-the-futuristic-sounds-of-sun.text:
The Futuristic Sounds of Sun Ra is the fourth studio album by Sun Ra and his Arkestra. It was recorded on 10 October 1961 for Savoy and came out in 1962. Tom Wilson supervised. It was the first record by a slimmed-down Arkestra, after the bandleader and the core of the group had moved from Chicago to New York. The recording took place at Medallion Studio in Newark.

He plays acoustic piano throughout the record. Various percussion instruments give some tracks a touch of the exotic. Except for The Beginning, all the pieces are very accessible. China Gates was written by Victor Young, the rest by the bandleader himself. Distribution was poor and no reviews appeared for years. In 1984 the album was reissued as We Are in the Future. It is regarded as one of the most accessible records in his large body of work.
werk/sun-ra-the-futuristic-sounds-of-sun.listen: Listen to Tapestry from an Asteroid and notice how the piano and the percussion together give a distinctive tone colour.

werk/suzanne-vega-days-of-open-hand.text:
Days of Open Hand is Suzanne Vega's third studio album and came out on 10 April 1990 on A&M Records, as the follow-up to the successful Solitude Standing. She produced it together with Anton Sanko, who co-composed six of the eleven songs. The recording took place from late 1989 to early 1990 in studios in New York. The folk rock was given more variety, with instruments such as the ney and the dumbec, more synthesizers and samplers, and guests such as Philip Glass, Shawn Colvin and John Linnell of They Might Be Giants.

The album did well in the British top 10, but in the United States it stalled at number 50, without a major hit. Even so, more than a million copies were sold. It won a Grammy for best packaging. Paul Evans in Rolling Stone gave it four out of five stars and called it her hardest and most beautiful music to date.
werk/suzanne-vega-days-of-open-hand.listen: Listen to Fifty-Fifty Chance (Fifty Fifty), whose strings were arranged by Philip Glass, and notice the atmosphere the song builds.

werk/suzanne-vega-nine-objects-of-desire.text:
Nine Objects of Desire was released on 10 September 1996 on A&M Records and is Suzanne Vega's fifth album. Mitchell Froom, then her husband, produced it, as he did its predecessor 99.9F°. The recording took place at The Magic Shop in New York. The music features experimental instrumentation and arrangements, with influences from jazz, bossa nova and alternative rock. The lyrics are more personal than before, with fewer characters and more of her own life.

Birth-Day (Love Made Real) is about the birth of her daughter Ruby. Caramel is strongly influenced by bossa nova and by the music of Astrud Gilberto and was given a feeling of Antônio Carlos Jobim. She calls it one of her proudest songs. Reviews were positive, although the album sold less than earlier records. No Cheap Thrill became a hit in the United Kingdom.
werk/suzanne-vega-nine-objects-of-desire.listen: Listen to Caramel and notice the bossa nova influence in the rhythm and atmosphere of the song.

werk/suzanne-vega-solitude-standing.text:
Solitude Standing is Suzanne Vega's second studio album, released in April 1987 on A&M Records. Steve Addabbo and Lenny Kaye produced it. It became her most commercially successful and most critically acclaimed album. It reached number 11 on the Billboard 200 and number 2 on the British chart, and went platinum in the United States and Britain.

The album opens with Tom's Diner a cappella and closes with an instrumental version. In 1990 a remix of the song by the producers of DNA reached number one in the United Kingdom. Night Vision comes from a poem by Paul Éluard, Calypso from the Odyssey. Rolling Stone found it less focused than the debut, but heard a singer and writer who was growing. AllMusic later called it a triumph: an album of story songs in widely varying musical settings.
werk/suzanne-vega-solitude-standing.listen: Listen to Tom's Diner (A Cappella), with which the album opens, and then compare it with Tom's Diner (Reprise) at the end: what is left without a voice?

werk/suzanne-vega-suzanne-vega.text:
Suzanne Vega is the debut album of the American singer-songwriter Suzanne Vega. It was released on 1 May 1985 on A&M Records. The recordings were largely made at Celestial Sound in New York, under Steve Addabbo and Lenny Kaye. The album departs from what was usual at the time: the arrangements are sparse and folk-like. It helped usher in a new era of singer-songwriters.

The success exceeded expectations. In the United States more than two hundred thousand copies were sold, in the United Kingdom many more. Marlene on the Wall, Small Blue Thing and Knight Moves were released as singles. Marlene on the Wall became a big hit in England only after a reissue in 1986. Rolling Stone later placed the album at number 80 among the best records of the 1980s, and a reviewer in Spin called it a strong introduction.
werk/suzanne-vega-suzanne-vega.listen: Listen to Marlene on the Wall to hear how the acoustic guitar and the soft, flat voice tell many stories with few means.

werk/sweet-desolation-boulevard.text:
Desolation Boulevard is the third studio album by Sweet, released in Britain in November 1974. Two distinctly different versions exist. In Europe, RCA released a version containing the song Turn It Down and the original recording of Fox on the Run. In May 1975 Capitol released a different version in the United States, with Ballroom Blitz and the single version of Fox on the Run. There the album reached twenty-fifth place.

The European version includes, among others, The Six Teens, Solid Gold Brass and Medussa, and a version of My Generation by The Who. The Man with the Golden Arm lasts almost nine minutes. Guitarist Andy Scott said that such variety proves the band never followed a fixed recipe. The cover was made by Hipgnosis, known for Pink Floyd. The photograph was taken at a rock club on Sunset Boulevard.
werk/sweet-desolation-boulevard.listen: Listen to Fox on the Run and notice the structure and the harmony vocals. Then compare it with The Man with the Golden Arm, which lasts much longer and takes up more room.

werk/sweet-funny-how-sweet-co-co-can-be.text:
Funny How Sweet Co-Co Can Be is the debut album by Sweet, which came out on RCA in November 1971. Most of the songs were written and produced by the duo Mike Chapman and Nicky Chinn. In addition, the band wrote a few songs themselves, such as Honeysuckle Love and Jeanie. The album also contains cover versions, such as Reflections by Holland, Dozier and Holland and Daydream by John Sebastian.

Two singles were hits in Britain: Funny Funny reached thirteenth place in March 1971 and Co-Co second in June. In the United States only Co-Co made the chart. In Finland the album topped the chart in February 1972. In West Germany it was released under the title Funny Funny, How Sweet Co-Co Can Be, with a different cover and an extra track, Done Me Wrong All Right.
werk/sweet-funny-how-sweet-co-co-can-be.listen: Listen to Co-Co and notice how simple and singable the melody is. Also hear how the band then plays a familiar song in its own style with Reflections.

werk/syd-barrett-the-madcap-laughs.text:
Syd Barrett left Pink Floyd in April 1968, after his behaviour had become increasingly erratic. Recording for his first solo record began in May 1968 under Peter Jenner at EMI Studios, but went badly. Barrett suddenly stopped and ended up in psychiatric care. In early 1969 he took up his music again, and Malcolm Jones of the label Harvest took over the production.

The bulk of the record was made between April and July 1969. In total five producers were credited, including Barrett himself and his former bandmates David Gilmour and Roger Waters. Among the guest musicians were members of Soft Machine. The album was released in January 1970 on Harvest and reached position 40 on the British chart. In the United States it followed only in 1974.
werk/syd-barrett-the-madcap-laughs.listen: Listen to the voice and the guitar in Octopus and notice how sparse the accompaniment is.

werk/t-i-i-m-serious.text:
In 1999 the Atlanta rapper T.I. was discovered by Kawan KP Prather, whose label Ghet-O-Vision belonged to LaFace Records. His debut album was released on 9 October 2001 on Arista Records, after LaFace had been dissolved and folded into Arista. Guests include Pharrell Williams of the Neptunes, Jazze Pha, Too Short and Lil Jon. Many songs are about his time as a drug dealer, something he was as a teenager.

The album sold modestly and reached number 98 on the Billboard 200. Reviewers were divided: some found many songs similar to each other, others praised the detailed stories. The title song, produced by the Neptunes with Beenie Man, did not make the Hot 100, but did well locally. After the disappointing figures, he proposed to Arista that they form a joint venture or let him go. The label chose the latter.
werk/t-i-i-m-serious.listen: Listen to Still Ain't Forgave Myself, a song that a reviewer called surprisingly tender, and notice the storytelling tone of the lyrics.

werk/t-i-king.text:
King is T.I.'s fourth studio album and was released on 28 March 2006 on Grand Hustle and Atlantic. It was first intended as the soundtrack to his film debut ATL, but he had so much material that it also became an album in its own right. The title refers to his son, Clifford King Joseph Harris III. The recording took a year and a half and more than 70 songs were made. Producers included DJ Toomp, Cool & Dre, Just Blaze, Mannie Fresh and Swizz Beatz. Common took over the guest role from Jay-Z, who could not do it because of his schedule.

What You Know became the big hit: number 3 on the Billboard Hot 100 and a Grammy for Best Rap Solo Performance. The album debuted at number 1 on the Billboard 200 and was praised for its varied style, its lavish production and the contradictory themes in the lyrics. It ranked high on several year-end lists.
werk/t-i-king.listen: Listen to What You Know and notice the production by DJ Toomp, for which critics had the most praise.

werk/t-i-trap-muzik.text:
After the disappointing sales of I'm Serious, the rapper T.I. was dropped by Arista. In 2002 he started his own label Grand Hustle with Jason Geter and signed with Atlantic Records. Trap Muzik came out on 19 August 2003, with DJ Toomp as executive producer. Producers also included David Banner, Jazze Pha and Kanye West. Guests include 8Ball and MJG, Bun B and Mac Boney.

With the title he points to the trap, the place where drugs are sold. He wanted to show life there from all sides. The singles 24's, Be Easy, Rubber Band Man and Let's Get Away became hits. Rubber Band Man stood out for a rising organ riff by David Banner. The album entered at number 4 on the Billboard 200 and went platinum. The reviews were favourable and saw it as a considerable improvement on his debut.
werk/t-i-trap-muzik.listen: Listen to Rubber Band Man and notice the rising organ riff that carries the song.

werk/t-i-urban-legend.text:
Urban Legend is T.I.'s third studio album and was released on 30 November 2004 on Atlantic Records and his own label Grand Hustle. In March 2004 an arrest warrant had been issued against him for violating his probation. He was given three years in prison, but thanks to a work-release arrangement was allowed to carry on making music and recorded material for several albums in Atlanta and Los Angeles. Producers such as DJ Toomp, Jazze Pha, Lil Jon, The Neptunes, Mannie Fresh, Scott Storch and Swizz Beatz worked on it.

Bring Em Out became his first top 10 hit on the Billboard Hot 100, and U Don't Know Me reached number 23 and received a Grammy nomination. The album entered at number seven on the Billboard 200 and went platinum. Critics were mostly positive. AllMusic felt that he was repeating himself, and Rolling Stone called the production almost joyless, but regarded him as a top lyricist.
werk/t-i-urban-legend.listen: Listen to Bring Em Out and notice how the rapper lands his lyrics on a hefty drum pattern.

werk/t-rex-electric-warrior.text:
In the spring of 1971 T. Rex was riding a wave of success. Ride a White Swan and Hot Love were hits in England, and Marc Bolan had appeared on television in a silver suit with glitter under his eyes, which gave glam rock its start. Recording began in March at Trident Studios in London and continued in Hollywood and New York, with Tony Visconti as producer. Visconti felt that the relaxed atmosphere in America gave the album its special feel.

Bolan now wrote about himself, about cars, women and boogie, instead of the poetic fantasy worlds of his earlier albums. The sound is electric and poppy, with tricks such as flanging, reversed guitars and tape loops. Guest musicians included Rick Wakeman on piano in Get It On, and Flo and Eddie sang the androgynous backing vocals. The album reached number one in England and is seen as a key record of glam rock.
werk/t-rex-electric-warrior.listen: Listen to Get It On and notice the boogie rhythms, Rick Wakeman's piano and the backing vocals of Flo and Eddie.

werk/t-rex-the-slider.text:
The Slider is the seventh studio album by T. Rex, released on 21 July 1972. The band was at the peak of its fame: the press called the fan hysteria T. Rextasy, and Electric Warrior was the best-selling album of 1971 in Britain. Producer Tony Visconti recorded it in Copenhagen and mainly at the Château d'Hérouville near Paris, to escape British tax laws. Marc Bolan felt he was more honest about himself here than ever.

Metal Guru opens the record. Spaceball Ricochet and Main Man are acoustic ballads, while Buick MacKane and Chariot Choogle sound heavier. Bolan called that Zep Rex. Telegram Sam and Metal Guru reached number one in Britain. The album reached number four in the United Kingdom and number seventeen in the United States. The first reviews were mixed, later ones mostly positive.
werk/t-rex-the-slider.listen: Listen to Metal Guru and notice the strings and the dreamy backing vocals around Bolan's voice.

werk/take-that-beautiful-world.text:
Beautiful World was released on 27 November 2006 and was Take That's first studio album in eleven years. It was also the first record as a quartet, without Robbie Williams, who had left in 1995. During the Ultimate Tour the four thought about a new album. They agreed that everyone would co-write and co-produce, and John Shanks was brought in as producer. For the first time every member sang lead on at least one song. The title was chosen by Howard Donald.

Patience was the first single and went to number one in Britain. It won a BRIT Award for best British single in 2007. Shine also became a number one. I'd Wait for Life ended a run of six number one hits. The reviews were very positive: the album breathed gratitude, and the songs were varied and more thoughtful than earlier work. It topped the chart in the United Kingdom and Ireland.
werk/take-that-beautiful-world.listen: Listen to Hold On, on which Mark Owen sings lead, and notice how the song sounds when the voice is not Gary Barlow's.

werk/take-that-everything-changes.text:
Everything Changes is the second studio album by Take That. It was the band's first to go to number 1 on the British album chart and was nominated for the 1994 Mercury Prize. It was one of the best-selling albums of 1993 in the United Kingdom.

With this album the group also broke through in Europe, where the record reached the top ten in many countries. It also did well in Australia and Japan. The album again contains songs by Gary Barlow and Howard Donald. It stayed in the British top 75 for a year and a half and received the Smash Hits award for best album. It opens with the title song and contains Relight My Fire, with Lulu, and Why Can't I Wake Up With You, a song the group had previously recorded as a ballad.
werk/take-that-everything-changes.listen: Listen to Relight My Fire and notice the way Lulu's voice alternates with the voices of the group.
